nodes.rationale: NdPr is the workhorse light REE for NdFeB permanent magnets used in servo motors, robotic actuators, EV traction motors, and humanoid joints. China dominates refining/separation at approximately 85-90% globally (USGS 2024; IEA Critical Minerals 2024). Magnet-grade NdPr cannot be substituted in high-energy-density applications without major performance penalty; ferrite alternatives sacrifice ~5x energy density. Qualification of alternative supply (Lynas Malaysia, MP Materials Mountain Pass) requires multi-year ramp. China's expanded REE export control regime (Oct 2024 / Apr 2025 dual-use list additions) and the consolidated China Rare Earth Group give Beijing pricing and allocation control. Meets all three CRITICAL criteria: concentration ≥70%, no substitute, multi-year qualification.
nodes.concentration: China approximately 85-90% of separated/refined NdPr (USGS 2024 estimate). Mining more diversified (US ~15%, Australia ~12%), but separation/oxide stage bottleneck remains in China.
nodes.substitution: No commercial substitute for high-coercivity NdFeB in compact high-torque applications. Ferrite or SmCo trade away energy density. Recycling nascent (<5% supply).
nodes.policy_context: China expanded REE export controls Oct 2024; consolidated three SOEs into China Rare Earth Group (2021); April 2025 dual-use export licensing tightened.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024/2025 indicate China hosts ~90% of refined rare earth supply; multiple 2025-2026 industry sources put China's NdPr refined share at 85-92%. China's MOFCOM/GAC Announcement No. 18 (April 4, 2025) added Sm, Gd, Tb, Dy, Lu, Sc, Y to dual-use export control list — light REEs (Nd, Pr) deliberately excluded (CSIS, IEA, RSIS analyses). Lynas Malaysia LAMP produces 5,000-6,000 t/yr NdPr oxide (10,500 tpa capacity post-upgrade); MP Materials produced 2,599 t NdPr oxide in 2025 (101% YoY growth, 1,994 t sold) per Q4/FY2025 results. Arafura Nolans targeting ~3,600 tpa NdPr oxide (pre-commissioning). Australian Office of the Chief Economist projects ~5,750 t Australian NdPr oxide output in 2025 (+78% YoY). NdFeB substitution remains commercially infeasible for high-torque compact applications (servos, humanoid joints, EV traction); ferrite/SmCo sacrifice 4-5x energy density. Recycling <5% of supply. Calibration: NdPr matches Gallium HIGH anchor pattern (very high China concentration but recyclate/diversification underway + ex-China qualified supply scaling) rather than Dysprosium CRITICAL anchor (≥99% China + binding Dec 2024 export controls explicitly targeting it + no qualified non-China supply at scale). Two-of-three CRITICAL criteria → HIGH per framework rule.

nodes.rationale: Reference anchor for CRITICAL. Dy is essential for high-temperature stabilization of NdFeB magnets in EV traction motors and robotic servos operating above ~80C. China controls approximately 99% of global Dy separation and refining (USGS 2024; IEA). December 2024 China export controls explicitly named heavy REEs including Dy, requiring end-use licensing. No commercial substitute — grain-boundary diffusion reduces Dy loading but does not eliminate requirement. Qualification of non-Chinese Dy (Lynas heavy REE circuit, Iluka Eneabba) is 3-5 years out. Removal would halt high-temp magnet production globally within 1-2 quarters.
nodes.concentration: China approximately 99% of separated Dy (USGS 2024). Myanmar feed ~50% of Chinese imports — Kachin region disruptions amplify risk.
nodes.substitution: None at scale. Dy-free magnet R&D (Niron Magnetics iron nitride) is pre-commercial. Grain boundary diffusion reduces but does not eliminate Dy need.
nodes.policy_context: China export controls Dec 2024 (heavy REEs); April 2025 dual-use list additions; Myanmar Kachin supply disruptions 2024-2025.
nodes.verifier_evidence: All three CRITICAL bars verified against current (May 2026) evidence: (1) Concentration ≥70%: China still controls approximately 99% of separated heavy REE / Dy refining — Wuxi remains the dominant refining hub, with Lynas Malaysia's May 2025 first commercial Dy oxide production representing under 5% of global supply (projected to reach only 15-20% by 2030 per industry forecasts). USGS 2025 Critical Minerals List ranks Dy as highest-risk REE. (2) No commercial substitute today: Grain boundary diffusion reduces Dy loading 70-100% on lower-grade NdFeB but does NOT eliminate Dy need for high-temperature (>80C) traction motor and servo grades. Niron Magnetics iron nitride remains pre-commercial — first plant initial operations late 2025/early 2026, EV/robotics prototypes only debuted at CES 2026 with Bimotal and MATTER; not qualified at scale for high-temp automotive traction. (3) Multi-year qualification: 3-5 years for non-Chinese Dy (Lynas heavy REE circuit, Iluka Eneabba) to reach material share. Policy basis is intact: April 4, 2025 MOFCOM/GAC Announcement No. 18 added Dy to dual-use export control list and remains OPERATIVE — the November 2025 suspension applied only to the October 9, 2025 controls, not the April controls (per Pillsbury, Clark Hill, Morrison Foerster legal analyses). IEA recorded European Dy/Tb prices at six times Chinese domestic equivalent at peak disruption. Calibration is consistent with framework anchor (Dy = CRITICAL).

nodes.rationale: Sm is the feedstock for SmCo magnets used in high-temperature defense/aerospace applications (radar, missile actuators, satellites) and some robotic high-temp applications where NdFeB cannot operate (>200C). China controls >95% of Sm separation (USGS 2024). April 2025 China export controls explicitly added samarium to the licensing list — a notable escalation specifically targeting Western defense supply chains. SmCo magnets are not substitutable in the high-temp niche; NdFeB+Dy cannot reach the same operating envelope. Qualification of ex-China Sm is constrained by Sm's economics (low natural abundance in monazite/bastnasite cuts; uneconomic standalone). Meets all three CRITICAL criteria with explicit recent policy weaponization.
nodes.concentration: China >95% of separated Sm (USGS 2024 estimate).
nodes.substitution: No substitute for high-temp magnet niche. NdFeB cannot replace SmCo above ~200C.
nodes.policy_context: China April 2025 export controls explicitly named Sm (along with Dy, Tb, Gd, Lu, Y, Sc) — direct Western defense supply chain targeting.
nodes.verifier_evidence: CONCENTRATION (PASSES >=70% bar): China controls ~90-95% of separated samarium supply chain (USGS-aligned industry reporting, RareEarthExchanges 2025). China holds ~35% of global reserves but >60% of output, with near-total dominance of separation/refining infrastructure. EX-CHINA QUALIFICATION (PASSES multi-year bar): Lynas Malaysia HREE facility achieved FIRST samarium oxide production March 2026 — small-scale milestone, not commercial defense-qualified supply. MP Materials Mountain Pass heavy rare earth separation facility targets mid-2026 commissioning with Sm production downstream of Dy/Tb. Defense qualification of SmCo magnet feedstock typically requires 2-4 years beyond first production. POLICY (BINDING, NOT SYMBOLIC): China MOFCOM Announcement No. 18 of 2025 (April 4, 2025) explicitly added samarium to medium/heavy rare earth licensing controls alongside Dy, Tb, Gd, Lu, Y, Sc. CSIS and Taylor Wessing analysis confirm enforcement via per-shipment MOFCOM licensing; TechTimes May 2026 reports controls "still bite" post-Beijing summit. Direct parallel to the Dy/Dec 2024 regime that anchors CRITICAL. SUBSTITUTION (NONE FOR NICHE): NdFeB caps at ~150-200C operating temperature even with heavy Dy loading; SmCo5 handles 300C, Sm2Co17 handles 550C. No commercial drop-in replacement for >200C magnet applications. CALIBRATION VS Dy ANCHOR: Sm sits just below Dy on concentration (90-95% vs >99%) but on the SAME April 2025 export control list and with the SAME no-substitute structure for its niche. Consistent with CRITICAL anchor.

nodes.rationale: Battery-grade Li is essential for EV/grid storage and robotic battery packs. Mining is geographically diversified (Australia ~47%, Chile ~25%, China ~18% — USGS 2024), but China controls approximately 65-70% of lithium chemical refining (carbonate and hydroxide). Substitution is constrained near-term: sodium-ion is scaling (CATL, BYD 2024-2025 commercial product) but lower energy density limits humanoid/robotic high-power applications. Multiple non-Chinese refining projects (Albemarle, SQM, Pilbara/POSCO, Tianqi-Kwinana) are scaling. Does not meet CRITICAL: mining diversified, refining concentration is high but not ≥70% sole-country at sufficient confidence, and substitution paths (LFP chemistry reduces Ni/Co dependency; Na-ion emerging) within 2-3 year horizon for non-premium applications.
nodes.concentration: Mining diversified (Australia ~47%, Chile ~25%, China ~18%). Refining: China approximately 65-70% of chemical conversion (IEA 2024).
nodes.substitution: Sodium-ion commercial (CATL, BYD 2024-2025) but lower energy density. No substitute for high-energy-density Li-ion in mobile robotics.
nodes.policy_context: Chile lithium nationalization framework (2023); US IRA FEOC rules excluding Chinese-refined Li from credits (2024); no export controls on Li yet.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS 2024 confirms mining diversification (Australia ~47%, Chile ~25%, China ~18%) — the upstream commodity is NOT concentrated. IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024 places China at ~65% of refined lithium chemicals, which is the lower bound of the proposal's range and sits mid-band (not top) of HIGH's "typically 50-70%" criterion. Critically, ex-China refining has commercial scale today: Albemarle Kemerton (WA), Tianqi-IGO Kwinana (WA), SQM (Chile), POSCO Gwangyang (Korea), Livent/Allkem (now Arcadium) — these are operational, not just announced. Sodium-ion has moved from lab to commercial product in 2024-2025: CATL Naxtra (Q2 2025 mass production), BYD Seagull (2024 deployments), HiNa Battery commercial cells — substitution is materially stronger than at original framework calibration. There are NO export controls on lithium (contrast with Gallium's Dec 2024 controls anchoring HIGH); Chile's 2023 nationalization framework affects mining (already diversified), not refining. IRA FEOC rules redirect credits but do not constrain supply. Calibration: vs. Gallium (HIGH @ ~98% China primary + binding export controls + no substitute), lithium at ~65% refining + no controls + commercial Na-ion substitute is meaningfully less acute. Lithium tracks the SiC MEDIUM anchor closely: "concentration exists but viable substitution paths or diversification underway; commercial alternatives within 2-3 year qualification reach" — multiple ex-China refiners are already past the 2-3yr qualification horizon. Per the framework's anti-fabrication rule (default to MEDIUM/LOW if concentration unclear, never default to HIGH/CRITICAL) and skeptical posture for borderline calls, the appropriate rating is MEDIUM.

nodes.rationale: DRC produces approximately 70-74% of mined Co (USGS 2024); China refines approximately 70-75% of cobalt sulfate for batteries (IEA 2024). Battery sub-field bottleneck is real for NMC chemistries, but LFP cathode substitution (now >40% of global EV battery deployment, BNEF 2024) is materially reducing Co intensity. CMOC (Chinese-owned) acquisition of Tenke Fungurume and Kisanfu in DRC further consolidates Chinese influence over the mining stage. Two-of-three CRITICAL criteria (concentration + qualification time) but viable substitution (LFP) for many applications keeps this at HIGH. Cobalt remains essential for high-energy-density applications (humanoid actuator packs, aerospace).
nodes.concentration: DRC approximately 70-74% mining (USGS 2024). China approximately 70-75% refined cobalt sulfate (IEA 2024). CMOC Chinese ownership of DRC mines amplifies.
nodes.substitution: LFP cathode displacing NMC in low-mid energy applications. High-Ni/low-Co NMC (NMC 9.5.5) reducing intensity. No substitute in high-energy aerospace.
nodes.policy_context: DRC export bans periodic; Indonesian Co byproduct from HPAL Ni adding non-DRC supply; US IRA FEOC rules excluding Chinese refining.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS 2024 confirms DRC ~70-74% mined Co share and IEA 2024 confirms China ~75% refined cobalt sulfate — concentration figures are accurate. However, the proposal overstates the bottleneck severity relative to the HIGH anchor (gallium). Key refutation points: (1) LFP cathodes now exceed 40% of global EV battery deployment (BNEF 2024) and are displacing NMC in most volume applications — this is a commercial, qualified substitute at scale, materially stronger substitution than the gallium case. (2) Indonesian HPAL nickel byproduct adds ~30-40 kt/yr non-DRC cobalt supply (Sumitomo, Vale, Huayou projects), diversifying mining concentration. (3) No binding export-control regime exists on cobalt comparable to China's July 2023 gallium/germanium controls or December 2024 dysprosium controls — DRC export bans are periodic and intermittent. (4) Cobalt prices collapsed ~60% from 2022 peaks through 2024, reflecting oversupply from Indonesian ramp and LFP-driven demand destruction — markets are not pricing a binding shortage. (5) Multi-supplier refining base (Glencore, Umicore, Sumitomo, Huayou, CMOC) provides further diversification. CRITICAL criteria check: concentration YES, no substitute FAILS (LFP at scale), multi-year qualification FAILS (LFP already qualified). Only 1 of 3 CRITICAL bars met. Against the SiC MEDIUM anchor (multi-supplier with capex scaling) cobalt's posture is comparable — concentrated but with active diversification and commercial substitution within reach. Against the Ga HIGH anchor (98% concentration + binding controls + limited recyclate) cobalt is materially less acute. MEDIUM is the calibrated rating.

nodes.rationale: Indonesia HPAL (high-pressure acid leach) and matte conversion capacity surge (Tsingshan, CATL, GEM) has shifted Class 1 battery-grade Ni supply meaningfully. Indonesia now approximately 55% of global mined Ni (USGS 2024), with Class 1 conversion via Chinese-led HPAL projects. While concentration risk exists (Indonesian + Chinese-financed), the underlying commodity is LME-traded with substantial Russian, Canadian, Australian, and Filipino supply. LFP substitution displacing high-Ni cathodes in low-end EVs. Does not meet CRITICAL: multi-country production, fungible at Class 2 stage, LFP substitution path. Concentration concern is geopolitical (Chinese capex dominance in Indonesia) rather than physical.
nodes.concentration: Indonesia approximately 55% of mined Ni (USGS 2024); Chinese-financed HPAL dominates Class 1 conversion. Russia/Canada/Australia retain non-Chinese Class 1 production.
nodes.substitution: LFP cathode displaces high-Ni NMC in commodity EV. No substitute for high-Ni aerospace alloys (Inconel).
nodes.policy_context: Indonesia ore export ban (2020); Inflation Reduction Act FEOC restrictions on Chinese-owned Indonesian Ni (2024); LME nickel trading suspension precedent (March 2022).

nodes.rationale: High-purity manganese sulfate monohydrate (HPMSM, >99.9% purity for cathode use) is China-dominated at approximately 90-95% of global production capacity (Benchmark Mineral Intelligence 2024). Standard Mn ore is multi-country and fungible (South Africa ~36%, Gabon, Australia — USGS 2024), but the HPMSM sub-field is sole-source concentrated. Substitution: rising LMFP and Mn-rich cathodes (Tesla, Ford pursuing high-Mn) actually increase HPMSM demand; non-Chinese HPMSM capacity (Element 25 Australia, Euro Manganese Czech Republic, South32 Hermosa) is pre-commercial through 2026-2027. Two-of-three CRITICAL criteria (concentration + multi-year qualification); raw ore alternative exists but conversion bottleneck remains.
nodes.concentration: HPMSM (battery-grade): China approximately 90-95% (Benchmark Mineral Intelligence 2024). Mn ore: South Africa ~36%, multi-country.
nodes.substitution: No substitute in cathode chemistry where Mn-rich is required. Standard Mn ore widely available; bottleneck is purification.
nodes.policy_context: USGS added Mn to critical minerals list 2022; US DOE awarded HPMSM grants 2023-2024 (South32, Element 25); no export controls yet.
nodes.verifier_evidence: HPMSM concentration of ~90-95% China is corroborated by Benchmark Mineral Intelligence and CRU 2023-2024 estimates — credible and current. The figure tracks the sulfate purification chokepoint, which is distinct from raw Mn ore (multi-country: SA ~36%, Gabon, Australia, Brazil per USGS 2024). Ex-China HPMSM capacity (Element 25 Louisiana DOE-backed plant ~2026, Euro Manganese Bécov ~2027, South32 Hermosa) is genuinely pre-commercial, with cathode qualification cycles adding 12-18 months on top — meeting the multi-year qualification bar. Substitution dynamics actually worsen the bottleneck: Tesla/Ford/GM Mn-rich (LMR, LMFP, high-Mn NMC) adoption increases HPMSM demand rather than offering an off-ramp. Recyclate path is nascent for Mn (unlike Ni/Co). USGS critical minerals 2022 listing and DOE grants to South32 (~$21M Sept 2023) and Element 25 (~$115M 2022) verified. Calibration check: profile closely matches Gallium HIGH anchor (China ~98% primary, ex-China capacity scaling) — HPMSM is slightly less acute (no binding export controls yet) but stronger demand tailwind, balancing out. Does NOT clear CRITICAL: only 2 of 3 bars (concentration + multi-year qualification met; "no substitute today" bar borderline since raw ore is multi-country and some non-Mn-rich chemistries exist). Does NOT warrant MEDIUM downgrade: viable commercial substitution is NOT within 2-3 year reach when qualification cycles are included.

nodes.rationale: China produces approximately 77-80% of mined natural graphite (USGS 2024) and approximately 95% of spherical graphite (anode-grade) and synthetic graphite anode material (BNEF 2024). China imposed export controls on certain graphite items Dec 2023, citing national security. Silicon anode and Si-C composite are scaling (Sila Nano, Group14, Amprius) but remain <5% of anode market through 2026 and do not eliminate graphite need. Non-Chinese spherical/synthetic anode capacity (Syrah Resources Vidalia LA, POSCO Future M, Northern Graphite) is qualifying but multi-year. Boundary case — concentration is CRITICAL-level but Si anode substitution path within 3-year horizon and ongoing diversification keep this at HIGH.
nodes.concentration: China approximately 77-80% mined natural graphite (USGS 2024); approximately 95% spherical and synthetic anode material (BNEF 2024).
nodes.substitution: Silicon and Si-C composite anodes scaling (Sila, Group14, Amprius) — pre-commercial volume. No full substitute for graphite in commodity Li-ion.
nodes.policy_context: China graphite export controls Dec 2023 (licensing for spherical and certain synthetic items); US DOE IRA grants for non-China anode capacity (Syrah, Novonix).
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025 confirms China produced 1.27Mt of 1.63Mt global natural graphite in 2024 (78% share), matching the proposal's 77-80% figure. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence and MMTA confirm China controls >90% of spherical graphite and anode active material, consistent with the cited ~95% BNEF figure. China's MOFCOM/GAC export control regime on high-purity synthetic graphite and natural flake graphite (including spherical and expanded) took effect Dec 1, 2023 (announced Oct 20, 2023) and is binding: Fastmarkets reports Jan-Feb 2024 spherical graphite exports fell 64.5% YoY (7,240t to 2,567t), with permit processing extended to 30-40 days — real enforcement, not symbolic. Silicon anode substitution remains pre-commercial: Sila Nanotechnologies' Moses Lake facility targets only 10 GWh by 2026; total silicon anode battery market was ~$500M in 2025 vs. a multi-hundred-billion-dollar Li-ion market — well under 5% penetration, confirming the proposer's claim. Syrah Resources Vidalia is operating at just 11.25ktpa AAM (with 45ktpa FID pending) and POSCO Future M qualification is multi-year — material diversification but small vs. China's dominance. Calibration check: this maps closely to the Gallium HIGH anchor (high concentration + binding export controls + ex-China qualification underway). Does not meet CRITICAL — the Dec 2023 controls are a licensing regime, not an embargo, supply continues flowing with permits, and ex-China commercial spherical/AAM capacity (Syrah, Posco) exists at small scale today, preventing the 1-2 quarter halt threshold required by the Dy anchor. Does not warrant MEDIUM — unlike the SiC anchor, there is no multi-supplier ex-China commercial AAM market at scale today. HOLD at HIGH.

nodes.rationale: Tantalum capacitors are critical for high-reliability electronics (aerospace, medical, defense, AI server boards). Mining concentration is DRC/Rwanda (approximately 50% combined — USGS 2024) with conflict-mineral compliance overhead, but supply has diversified meaningfully: Brazil, Ethiopia, Australia (Pilbara byproduct), and Canada provide non-Central-African supply. Class-leading capacitor manufacturers (KEMET, AVX, Vishay) maintain strategic inventories. Substitution: MLCC ceramic and polymer aluminum capacitors substitute in lower-reliability roles, but not for the highest-reliability niches. No recent export controls. Does not meet CRITICAL — no single country ≥70%, and substitution within sub-niche exists.
nodes.concentration: DRC + Rwanda approximately 50% mined (USGS 2024). Brazil, Australia (byproduct), Ethiopia provide non-conflict supply.
nodes.substitution: MLCC and polymer-Al capacitors substitute in many roles. Ta capacitors irreplaceable for high-volumetric-efficiency military/medical.
nodes.policy_context: Dodd-Frank Section 1502 conflict-mineral disclosure (DRC adjacent); no export controls.

nodes.rationale: Brazil produces approximately 88-90% of global Nb, with CBMM (Companhia Brasileira de Metalurgia e Mineração) alone producing approximately 80% (USGS 2024). Single-country, near-sole-source structure. However, Brazil is a friendly jurisdiction (US/Japan/EU/Korea aligned), CBMM is privately held with stable long-term offtakes, and a secondary source exists (Niobec, Quebec, Canada — Magris Resources). Nb is used in HSLA steel, superalloys (jet engines, gas turbines), and Nb-Ti superconductors (MRI, particle accelerators, quantum). Substitution: vanadium in some HSLA grades; molybdenum partially in superalloys. Two-of-three CRITICAL criteria (concentration + qualification time) but friendly-jurisdiction concentration and partial substitutability keep this at HIGH rather than CRITICAL.
nodes.concentration: Brazil approximately 88-90% mined; CBMM single-company approximately 80% (USGS 2024). Niobec (Canada) secondary.
nodes.substitution: Vanadium in some HSLA grades; molybdenum partial in superalloys. No substitute in Nb-Ti superconducting magnets (MRI, fusion).
nodes.policy_context: No export controls; Brazil-aligned with US/EU/Japan. CBMM equity stakes held by JFE/Nippon Steel/POSCO/CITIC consortiums.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024: Brazil produces ~88-92% of global niobium; CBMM ~80% single-firm share. Niobec (Magris Resources, Saint-Honore, Quebec) operational secondary source producing ferroniobium. CBMM equity: 15% Japanese-Korean consortium (JFE Steel, Nippon Steel, POSCO, NSSMC) acquired 2011; 15% Chinese consortium (CITIC, Anshan, Shougang, Taiyuan, Baosteel) acquired 2011 — creating multi-jurisdictional ownership and offtake alignment. No export-control regime exists on Nb (contrast: China Dec 2024 Dy export controls). Substitution: vanadium microalloying in HSLA steel is commercial standard (used in ~50% of microalloyed steel globally); molybdenum partial substitution in superalloys established; titanium nitride/carbide in some grades. Only Nb-Ti and Nb3Sn LTS superconductors lack near-term commercial substitutes, but REBCO/HTS emerging for high-field applications. Brazil is NATO-aligned via US strategic partnerships and EU trade agreements. Framework anchor mismatch: Gallium HIGH requires hostile jurisdiction + export controls + diversification underway; Niobium has friendly jurisdiction + no controls + diversification already operational at Niobec — this aligns with SiC MEDIUM anchor (concentration with viable multi-supplier substitution within 2-3 year reach).

nodes.rationale: China produces approximately 48-60% of mined Sb (USGS 2024) but controls a much higher share of processed/refined Sb (approximately 80%+ when including processing of Russian and Tajik ore). China's Aug 2024 export controls on Sb (effective Sep 15, 2024) caused immediate price spikes (>200% rally Sep 2024-Mar 2025) and Western supply scrambles. Antimony is essential for: lead-acid battery hardening, flame retardants, photovoltaic glass clarifying agent, and — critically for defense — armor-piercing ammunition, night vision, and nuclear weapons. No commercial substitute for many defense applications. Perpetua Resources (Stibnite, Idaho) is years from production. Following Dec 2024 China full ban on Sb/Ga/Ge exports to US, this meets all three CRITICAL criteria.
nodes.concentration: China approximately 48-60% mining (USGS 2024); >80% refined/processed when including processing of imported ore. Tajikistan, Russia secondary.
nodes.substitution: No substitute in defense applications (armor-piercing, night vision). Halogen-free flame retardants partial commercial substitute in plastics.
nodes.policy_context: China Aug 2024 export controls (effective Sep 15, 2024); Dec 3, 2024 China full export ban on Sb/Ga/Ge to United States.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024: China ~48% of global antimony mine production in 2023. IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025: China dominates refining for 19 of 20 minerals at ~70% average (antimony processing concentrated but not uniquely so). China MOFCOM Aug 14, 2024 export controls effective Sep 15, 2024; Dec 3, 2024 dual-use prohibition on Sb/Ga/Ge to US military users; Nov 10, 2025 suspension of prohibition until Nov 27, 2026 (CNBC, Fastmarkets, Pillsbury Law). Price action: $1,400/t (Jul 2024) → $38,000/t (Sep 2024) → $51,500-60,000/t (mid-2025) → ~$25,450/t FOB China and $34,000-35,500/t Rotterdam (Dec 2025); -18.1% Dec 2025-Mar 2026 (Fastmarkets, Argus, IMARC). Shadow supply: 3,834 metric tons of Sb oxides imported to US from Thailand/Mexico Dec 2024-Apr 2025, exceeding prior 3-year total (Quest Metals). Substitutes shipping: Tolsa ADINS at K 2025, NZC-FLMSYN-03 drop-in, FireBlend 33-A for PVC, Clariant Exolit OP phosphorus-based (Plastics Today, Clariant blog Jun 2025, NewZeal Chem). Robotics relevance: InSb is niche infrared detector material; Phlux's antimonide LiDAR raised £4m seed in 2022, not in mass production; AV LiDAR market dominated by silicon/InGaAs/CMOS (Semiconductor Today, Intel Market Research 2025). Perpetua Resources Stibnite Idaho mine years from production (confirmed in proposal). Anchor comparison: Dysprosium (CRITICAL) = >99% China refining + binding Dec 2024 controls + no NdFeB substitute; Antimony falls short on substitute availability and refining dominance.

nodes.rationale: China produces approximately 80-83% of mined W and approximately 85% of APT (ammonium paratungstate, the refined intermediate) globally (USGS 2024; ITIA 2024). WF6 (tungsten hexafluoride) is essential for semiconductor metallization (W plug, W word line in 3D NAND, contacts in logic) — sole-source semiconductor process gas with no substitute at current node geometries. China Feb 2025 export controls added tungsten products (including APT and specific tungsten compounds) to the dual-use list. Western APT capacity (Almonty Sangdong Korea, scheduled 2024-2025 ramp) is qualifying. WF6 supply (Versum/Merck, Linde, SK Materials) ultimately depends on W feedstock. Meets all three CRITICAL criteria: ≥70% concentration, no W substitute in semis, multi-year qualification.
nodes.concentration: China approximately 80-83% mined W; approximately 85% APT (USGS 2024). Almonty Sangdong (Korea) major non-China producer 2024-2025 ramp.
nodes.substitution: No substitute for W plug/contact in advanced logic and 3D NAND. Mo partial in some grades. Carbide tooling: PCD partial.
nodes.policy_context: China Feb 2025 export controls on W products (APT, W compounds, certain tungsten items added to dual-use export licensing).
nodes.verifier_evidence: VERIFIED: (1) USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025 reports China at 82.7-83% of 2024 mined tungsten (67,000t of 80,000t global), with Vietnam ~5.0% and Russia ~2.5% — comfortably above the ≥70% CRITICAL threshold. China share of APT refining estimated at ~85% (ITIA). (2) Feb 4, 2025 China MOFCOM/Customs Announcement No. 10 placed APT, tungsten oxides, and tungsten carbides on the dual-use licensing list under the Export Control Law — verified binding, not symbolic: APT export volumes fell from 782t in 2024 to 243t in first 11 months of 2025 (~70% YoY decline), confirmed by Fastmarkets and chemradar. (3) WF6 remains the standard semiconductor process gas for W metallization (plug, contact, 3D NAND word line); fluorine-free tungsten precursors and Mo substitution for word lines exist as multi-year R&D paths but are not drop-in at advanced nodes — qualification cycle is years. (4) Almonty Sangdong (Korea) began commercial mining 2025 with substantial completion, but ramp will take quarters and "non-China" base is only ~17-20%. All three CRITICAL bars cleared: ≥70% single-country (82.7% mining, ~85% APT), no commercial substitute at current geometries, multi-year qualification path. Calibrates with Dy CRITICAL anchor (China refining concentration + active export controls), and sits clearly above Ga HIGH anchor (where recyclate and diversification were further along). HOLD at CRITICAL.

nodes.rationale: Tin is critical for SnAgCu solder used in PCB assembly across all electronics (servers, robotics, semis). Mining is moderately concentrated: China approximately 22%, Indonesia approximately 18%, Myanmar approximately 14%, Peru approximately 8%, DRC approximately 6% (USGS 2024). Myanmar Wa State production disruption (Aug 2023 mining halt) and Indonesia export policy shifts created tight market. LME-traded with transparent pricing. Refining shifts to China (approximately 45% of refined tin) add concentration risk. No substitute for Sn in lead-free solder under RoHS. However, multi-country mining, LME fungibility, and recyclate availability prevent CRITICAL or HIGH rating. Does not meet CRITICAL: no single-country ≥70%, LME-traded.
nodes.concentration: Mining: China ~22%, Indonesia ~18%, Myanmar ~14%, Peru ~8% (USGS 2024). Refining: China ~45%.
nodes.substitution: No substitute for Sn in RoHS lead-free solder at current chemistries. Conductive adhesives niche-only.

nodes.rationale: Reference anchor for LOW. Copper is LME-traded, fully fungible commodity. Mining diversified: Chile ~24%, Peru ~10%, China ~8%, DRC ~12%, US ~5% (USGS 2024). Refining more concentrated in China (~42%) but global refining capacity (Chile, Japan, Korea, Zambia) is robust. Robotics, EV, datacenter, and electrification demand growth is driving structural deficit forecasts (Goldman, BHP estimating significant deficits by 2030+), but this is a price/quantity issue, not a bottleneck risk. Aluminum substitutes in transmission, HVAC, motor windings (partial). No concentration risk meaningful to AI-stack production continuity.
nodes.concentration: Mining: Chile ~24%, multi-country diversified (USGS 2024). Refining: China ~42%, Chile/Japan/Korea robust.
nodes.substitution: Aluminum substitutes partial in transmission and motors. No bottleneck — fungible LME commodity.
nodes.policy_context: No export controls; Chilean royalty/tax structure debates; long-term structural deficit forecast but not a near-term bottleneck.

nodes.rationale: LME-traded fungible commodity. Mining (bauxite) diversified: Australia ~28%, Guinea ~22%, China ~16%, Brazil ~9% (USGS 2024). Primary Al smelting concentrated in China (~58%) but ample non-Chinese capacity (Rusal, Rio Tinto, Alcoa, Norsk Hydro, Emirates Global Aluminium). High-purity Al sub-grades (4N+, used in semiconductor sputter targets and capacitor foil) have tighter supplier base (Sumitomo Chemical, Honeywell, Nippon Light Metal) — could be a sub-field bottleneck — but not at primary metal level. nodes.concentration: Bauxite: Australia ~28%, Guinea ~22% (USGS 2024). Primary Al smelting: China ~58%. Rusal/Rio Tinto/Alcoa/Norsk Hydro non-Chinese capacity.
nodes.substitution: Cu and steel substitute partial. No bottleneck at primary metal level.
nodes.policy_context: Russia Al sanctions (LME delivery restrictions 2024); China primary Al capacity cap policy; no export controls.

Industrial silver demand growth (solar PV silver paste, EV silver contacts, AI-stack PCB) is structural, but byproduct economics from Cu/Pb/Zn mining ensure ample supply response. PV silver paste thrifting (TOPCon/HJT cells reducing silver loading) actively underway. No concentration risk and no export controls. Could face price tightness from PV demand growth but no production-continuity bottleneck for AI stack.
nodes.concentration: Mexico ~24%, China ~14%, Peru ~14% (USGS 2024). Multi-country mining; LBMA/COMEX traded.
nodes.substitution: Copper for some industrial contacts; PV silver thrifting in TOPCon/HJT cells; aluminum metallization R&D pre-commercial.
nodes.policy_context: No export controls; structural deficit risk from PV demand 2025-2030 but not bottleneck.

nodes.rationale: China produces approximately 85-87% of global primary Mg (USGS 2024), concentrated in Shaanxi province. Mg is essential for lightweighting (humanoid robot structural frames, EV components, aerospace, electronics housings) and as aluminum alloying element. Sep 2021 Shaanxi power curtailments caused global Mg shortage with European auto production threatened — demonstrated bottleneck. Non-Chinese capacity (US Magnesium Utah, Magontec/Latrobe Magnesium Australia, Western Magnesium) is small relative to demand and ramping slowly. Substitution: Al substitutes partial in lightweighting (denser, less stiffness/weight), polymer composites in specific applications. Two-of-three CRITICAL criteria (≥70% concentration, qualification time); partial Al substitution prevents CRITICAL.
nodes.concentration: China approximately 85-87% of primary Mg (USGS 2024); approximately 50% from Shaanxi province (Yulin/Fugu area).
nodes.substitution: Al partial in lightweighting (denser); polymer composites in specific applications; no full substitute in lightest-weight structures.
nodes.policy_context: Sep-Oct 2021 Shaanxi power curtailment caused Mg crisis; no formal export controls but supply concentration severe.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024 confirms China at approximately 85-87% of global primary Mg production, concentrated in Shaanxi (Yulin/Fugu). Sep-Oct 2021 Shaanxi power curtailment is a documented real-world supply shock that threatened European auto production — demonstrates binding concentration risk. Ex-China capacity (US Magnesium Utah ~50kt, Latrobe Magnesium Australia, Magontec, Western Magnesium) is small relative to ~1Mt+ global demand and ramping slowly (multi-year qualification). Substitution: aluminum is partial substitute in lightweighting (denser ~2.7 vs 1.74 g/cm³, lower stiffness-to-weight) and polymer composites in niche applications — prevents CRITICAL but doesn't eliminate HIGH. Calibration check: above Ga anchor on concentration severity (Ga ~98% vs Mg ~86%) but Mg lacks formal export controls (key Ga distinguishing factor); 2021 crisis substitutes for export-control evidence by demonstrating real bottleneck. Clearly above SiC/MEDIUM anchor (which has multi-country supply). Two-of-three CRITICAL bars met (concentration + qualification time); partial Al substitution prevents CRITICAL elevation. HIGH is correctly calibrated.

nodes.rationale: Vanadium mining is concentrated in China (~70%), Russia (~17%), and South Africa (~8%) (USGS 2024). Primarily used as steel additive (HSLA, tool steels) where Nb partial substitute. Emerging demand from VRFB (vanadium redox flow batteries) for grid storage and superalloy aerospace. While Chinese mining concentration is high, South African (Bushveld Minerals — recent receivership challenges) and Brazilian (Largo Inc.) production provides non-Chinese supply. VRFB demand could tighten market but is pre-commercial at scale. Steel applications dominate consumption — substitution via Nb/Mo possible. Does not meet CRITICAL: substitutability in steel, multi-source supply (with Russia caveat post-2022), no recent export controls.
nodes.concentration: China ~70% mined V, Russia ~17%, South Africa ~8% (USGS 2024). Brazil (Largo) and Australia (Tivan) emerging.
nodes.substitution: Nb and Mo partial in steel alloys. VRFB has no substitute in flow battery sub-field — Zn-Br and Fe-Cr flow alternatives commercial but not drop-in.
nodes.policy_context: Russia sanctions complicate ~17% supply; no Chinese export controls on V; US DOE supporting VRFB scale-up.

nodes.rationale: China controls approximately 95-99% of separated Y supply (USGS 2024). Yttrium is essential for: YAG laser hosts (LiDAR, defense, fiber laser cutting), YSZ (yttria-stabilized zirconia) thermal barrier coatings on jet engine turbine blades, YBCO superconductors (fusion magnets, MRI), and as phosphor activator (Y2O3:Eu) in displays. April 2025 China export controls explicitly named yttrium among the seven REEs added to dual-use licensing. No substitute for Y in YAG laser host or YSZ TBC at current performance. Western Y separation capacity is minimal — Lynas and MP Materials focus on lighter REEs and Nd/Pr. Meets all three CRITICAL criteria with explicit Apr 2025 policy weaponization.
nodes.concentration: China approximately 95-99% separated Y (USGS 2024). Heavy REE separation almost entirely China-domestic; Myanmar feed important.
nodes.substitution: No substitute in YAG laser host, YSZ TBC, YBCO superconductors at current performance.
nodes.policy_context: China April 2025 export controls added Y (with Sm, Dy, Tb, Gd, Lu, Sc) to dual-use export licensing — direct Western defense/aerospace targeting.
nodes.verifier_evidence: Concentration verified: China ~90% of global Y supply, ~97% of mining produce, ~91% of REE refining capacity (USGS 2024/2025; multiple market trackers). U.S. has 100% net import reliance on Y, ~93% from China (2020-2023 avg, USGS). Policy verified and binding: April 4, 2025 MOFCOM dual-use export licensing covers seven heavy/medium REEs explicitly including yttrium (with Sm, Gd, Tb, Dy, Lu, Sc); regime "never suspended" and Chinese customs data shows Y exports ~50% below pre-restriction baseline (techtimes/Anderson Institute, 2026). Substitution: no commercial drop-in for YAG laser hosts in fiber/LiDAR lasers or YSZ TBCs on jet turbine blades at performance parity; alternatives (Nd:YVO4, Nd:YLF, rare-earth zirconates, hafnia-stabilized zirconia) require multi-year aerospace/laser qualification. Western separation capacity: Lynas Malaysia produces Dy oxide (May 2025) and Tb (June 2025) — first heavy REE separation outside China — but yttrium recovery is only planned for a future expansion phase beyond Apr 2026 Sm milestone. MP Materials focuses on Nd/Pr. All three CRITICAL bars satisfied: (1) ≥70% single-country share — 90-97% verified; (2) no commercial substitute today; (3) multi-year qualification path for alternatives. Calibration aligns with Dy CRITICAL anchor (same April 2025 control list, same separation bottleneck, comparable concentration). Sits above Ga HIGH anchor due to lack of recyclate channel and binding active export-licensing regime with measurable export reduction.

nodes.rationale: China produces approximately 80% of mined and refined Bi (USGS 2024). Primarily used in: low-melt fusible alloys (replacing Pb in RoHS), Bi2Te3 thermoelectric devices (Peltier cooling for laser diodes, semiconductor cooling, AI server thermal management), pharmaceuticals, and metallurgical additives. Bismuth byproduct of Pb/Cu/W mining — non-Chinese supply (Korea, Japan, Mexico) is small. No formal China export controls on Bi yet, but pattern of REE/Sb/Ga/Ge controls raises probability. Substitution: difficult in Bi2Te3 thermoelectric where it is the dominant commercial material; Pb-free solder uses Sn-Ag-Cu primary. Two-of-three CRITICAL criteria (≥70% concentration); absence of explicit export controls and limited substitution path keep at HIGH.
nodes.concentration: China approximately 80% of mined and refined Bi (USGS 2024). Byproduct of Pb/Cu/W; Korea, Japan, Mexico secondary.
nodes.substitution: Bi2Te3 dominant in commercial thermoelectric — no drop-in substitute. SnAgCu replaces Bi in solder.
nodes.policy_context: No formal export controls yet but China pattern of REE/Sb/Ga/Ge controls 2023-2025 raises probability.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024: China dominates refined Bi production (~70-80% range commonly cited). NO formal China export controls on bismuth as of May 2026 — distinct from Ga (Aug 2023 controls), Ge (Aug 2023), Sb (Sept 2024), graphite (Dec 2023), REE/W (2024-2025). Bi is byproduct of Pb/Cu/W smelting — secondary supply from Korea (LS-Nikko), Japan, Mexico, Bolivia exists but small. Bi2Te3 dominates commercial sub-200C thermoelectric (Peltier cooling for laser diodes, some datacenter thermal subsystems) — no drop-in substitute, but this is a niche application not foundational to AI silicon stack. Pb-free solder substitution to SnAgCu/SnCu is mature and commercial. Framework calibration: Gallium HIGH = ~98% concentration + binding 2023 export controls + direct AI-stack role (GaN power/RF). Bismuth has lower concentration, no binding controls, peripheral AI-stack role — falls short of HIGH anchor on two dimensions. Fits MEDIUM: concentration exists, partial substitution paths underway, no acute policy-driven supply shock today.

nodes.rationale: Public production data for Sc is genuinely thin — global production estimated at only ~25-30 tonnes/year (USGS 2024) with no transparent spot market. China and Russia are believed to be largest producers (NIOST estimates China ~66%, Russia ~26%, Philippines ~6%) but commercial trade is largely opaque bilateral. Sc-Al alloys (high-strength aerospace, sporting goods) and Sc-stabilized zirconia SOFC have niche applications. China April 2025 export controls included Sc in dual-use list, suggesting strategic relevance. Multiple non-Chinese projects (Rio Tinto Sorel-Tracy QC byproduct, Nyrstar Hobart byproduct, NioCorp Elk Creek Nebraska, Sunrise Energy Metals NSW) but commercial volumes uncertain. Frontier-stack volume genuinely speculative; physical AI stack demand pull is real (BMW/Airbus piloting Sc-Al) but not yet bottleneck-material. UNRATED is the calibration-honest output given thin public data and ambiguous cohort fit at current scale.
nodes.concentration: Estimated China ~66%, Russia ~26%, Philippines ~6% (NIOST 2023 estimate, not USGS-verified). Production ~25-30 t/yr — too thin for transparent share figures.
nodes.substitution: Sc-Al alloys substitutable by Ti or other Al alloys with weight penalty; SOFC YSZ partial substitute for ScSZ.
nodes.policy_context: China April 2025 export controls included Sc in dual-use list. Pentagon Sc-Al strategic stockpiling interest.

nodes.rationale: Heavy REE used (with Dy) for high-temperature stabilization of NdFeB magnets and as YAG/garnet activator for green phosphors. China controls >99% of Tb separation (USGS 2024) — essentially monopoly. Tb is rarer and more expensive than Dy ($800-1500/kg range, prone to thin-market price spikes). December 2024 China heavy REE export controls explicitly included Tb. No commercial substitute for high-temp magnet stabilization niche; grain boundary diffusion reduces but does not eliminate. Non-Chinese Tb supply (Lynas heavy REE circuit Malaysia, Iluka Eneabba Australia) is years from commercial Tb output. Pricing-thin status reinforces vulnerability — small allocation changes drive large price moves. Meets all three CRITICAL criteria; arguably the most concentrated REE bottleneck after Dy.
nodes.concentration: China >99% separated Tb (USGS 2024). Myanmar Kachin feedstock to Chinese separation.
nodes.substitution: No substitute for high-coercivity high-temp magnet stabilization. Tb-doped YAG phosphors substitutable for some color points.
nodes.policy_context: China December 2024 heavy REE export controls (with Dy); April 2025 dual-use list expansion (Sm/Dy/Tb/Gd/Lu/Y/Sc).
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS 2024 Mineral Commodity Summaries confirms China ~99% of separated heavy REE capacity including Tb (concentration well above 70% bar). MOFCOM Announcement 18 (April 4, 2025) explicitly added Tb to dual-use export control list alongside Sm/Gd/Dy/Lu/Sc/Y, building on December 3, 2024 heavy REE controls — licenses required and reportedly delayed/denied for Western OEMs in Q2 2025 (binding, not symbolic). No commercial substitute for high-coercivity high-temperature NdFeB stabilization in robotics servo motors and EV traction (N42SH/N48EH grades used in humanoid actuators); grain boundary diffusion reduces but does not eliminate Tb loading. Lynas Malaysia heavy REE circuit still ramping, Iluka Eneabba refinery delayed to 2026+, MP/Energy Fuels/Ucore all multi-year from commercial Tb separation — qualification path is 2-4 years minimum. NdFeB recyclate for Tb recovery is sub-5% globally, immaterial in 1-2Q horizon. Tb market is thinner than Dy (~400-500 t/yr vs ~1,200 t/yr) which arguably worsens vulnerability. Calibration consistency: Tb mirrors the Dy CRITICAL anchor (same concentration, same export regime, same substitution constraint) — downgrading would create framework inconsistency with the Dy reference case.

nodes.rationale: Semi-grade (11N+) polysilicon is dominated by Wacker (Germany), Hemlock (US), Tokuyama (Japan), OCI (Korea/Malaysia) — a multi-country oligopoly. Distinct from solar-grade (China-dominated). Capacity is concentrated but distributed across allied jurisdictions; no single-country chokepoint for semi-grade. Czochralski crystal pull is the downstream bottleneck more than raw poly.
nodes.concentration: Wacker/Hemlock/Tokuyama/OCI control ~80%+ of electronic-grade poly across Germany/US/Japan/Korea/Malaysia. No single country >50% for semi-grade specifically (China dominates solar-grade only).
nodes.substitution: No substitute for Si wafers in mainstream logic/memory; however, multi-supplier base across allied nations means substitution at the supplier level is viable within 1-2 quarters for most grades. Qualification for new poly source typically 6-12 months.
nodes.policy_context: Semi-grade poly is not under export-control regime targeting allied buyers. China's solar-grade poly faces UFLPA scrutiny (Xinjiang), but this is separate from electronic-grade supply.

nodes.rationale: China produces ~98% of primary gallium (USGS 2023-2024). July 2023 MOFCOM export controls require licenses for Ga/Ge exports; December 2024 expanded ban on exports to US. Substitution paths exist: recyclate from GaAs scrap, indium phosphide alternatives for some RF/optoelectronic applications, and capacity restarts in Hungary/Germany/Japan. Diversification underway but multi-year. Matches HIGH reference anchor exactly.
nodes.concentration: China ~98% of primary refined gallium (USGS 2024). Recycled supply adds ~30-40% to global availability outside China but does not displace primary dependence.
nodes.substitution: GaAs/GaN have no substitute in high-frequency RF, power amplifiers, and certain photonics; InP can substitute in some optoelectronic uses. Recycling and non-China primary capacity (Hungary, Germany, Japan, Kazakhstan) being restarted — qualification 2-3 years.
nodes.policy_context: China MOFCOM export licenses (July 2023); December 3, 2024 outright ban on exports to US for Ga/Ge/Sb dual-use applications.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024: China = 98% of primary low-purity gallium global production. USGS MCS 2025: 99% (https://pubs.usgs.gov/periodicals/mcs2025/mcs2025-gallium.pdf, https://pubs.usgs.gov/periodicals/mcs2024/mcs2024-gallium.pdf). MOFCOM Notice 2024 No. 46 (Dec 3, 2024) banned Ga/Ge/Sb dual-use exports to US (https://cset.georgetown.edu/publication/china-rare-earth-export-ban/). China MOFCOM suspended the ban Nov 9, 2025 until Nov 27, 2026, reverting to licensing regime; military end-user ban remains (https://www.cnbc.com/2025/11/09/china-suspends-ban-on-exports-of-gallium-germanium-antimony-to-us.html, https://www.fastmarkets.com/insights/china-suspends-export-prohibition-on-superhard-materials-us/). CSIS analysis: trade truce did NOT solve gallium problem (https://www.csis.org/analysis/us-china-trade-truce-has-not-solved-gallium-problem). Substitution: GaN-on-Si emerging but still Ga-dependent; InP partial substitute for optoelectronics but itself has ~70% supply-demand gap in 2025; "completely gallium-free solutions with comparable performance are still in the research stage." Non-China supply: Kazakhstan ERG starts Q3 2026 at 15 MT/yr; Germany announced restart but unscheduled; Japan + Russia remain only active non-China primary producers. Framework anchor for HIGH explicitly references Gallium with matching language: "~98% primary, but recyclate + diversification underway." Proposal aligns precisely with HIGH anchor calibration.

nodes.rationale: China ~60% of refined indium (USGS 2024); Korea, Japan, Canada also produce. ITO for displays and InP feedstock for photonics are downstream uses. Not under formal export-control regime as of mid-2025. Diversified supplier base outside China (Korea Zinc, Dowa, Teck) supports MEDIUM rating. InP wafer supply is more concentrated (Sumitomo, AXT) but substrate-level concern is downstream.
