nodes.substitution: ITO substitutes (silver nanowires, graphene) exist but lack commercial scale for high-end displays. InP has no direct substitute for high-speed photonics/100G+ optical transceivers. Diversified primary supply mitigates single-source risk.
nodes.policy_context: Not yet under China export controls as of May 2026; on watchlist following Ga/Ge precedent.

nodes.rationale: China ~60% of refined germanium (USGS 2024). July 2023 MOFCOM export controls (same regime as Ga); December 2024 US-targeted ban. Critical for IR optics (military), fiber optic dopants, SiGe wafers for RF, and PV (multi-junction space cells). Substitution limited in IR optics and SiGe. Concentration + export controls + limited substitution = HIGH (matches Ga anchor).
nodes.concentration: China ~60% refined Ge (USGS 2024); also produced from zinc byproduct in Canada (Teck), Belgium (Umicore), Russia. Primary mining limited; recycling ~30% of supply.
nodes.substitution: IR optics: ZnSe/ZnS partial substitutes but inferior. SiGe in RF: no substitute. Multi-junction PV: no substitute. Fiber doping: alternatives exist. 2-3 year qualification for alternative sources.
nodes.policy_context: China MOFCOM export licenses (July 2023); December 3, 2024 ban on exports to US for dual-use.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024 — Germanium: China ~60% of global refined output, US recycling/scrap ~30% of consumption. China MOFCOM July 2023 export licensing regime (parallel to Ga). December 3, 2024 China ban on Ge exports to US for dual-use applications. Ex-China producers: Teck Resources Trail Operations (Canada), Umicore Olen (Belgium), Nyrstar, and Russian zinc smelters produce Ge as zinc byproduct. Ge price spiked from ~$1,400/kg pre-controls to ~$2,800-3,500/kg through 2024 indicating real but absorbable supply stress. SiGe wafer and multi-junction PV cell substitution genuinely limited; IR optics have ZnSe/ZnS partial substitutes; fiber optic doping has alternatives. Framework anchors: Ga HIGH = ~98% China primary; SiC MEDIUM = multi-supplier concentrated with capex scaling. Ge at ~60% China + 3+ qualified ex-China byproduct sources + 30% recyclate aligns with SiC MEDIUM cohort, not Ga HIGH cohort.

nodes.rationale: Tellurium is byproduct of copper anode slime refining; supply tied to Cu refining geography. China leads (~50-60%) but Japan, Canada, Russia, Sweden also produce. CdTe PV (First Solar) is dominant end-use; semi uses (thermoelectrics, II-VI compounds) are smaller. Byproduct nature limits supply elasticity but multi-country base prevents CRITICAL/HIGH classification. Not under export controls.
nodes.concentration: China ~55% refined Te (USGS 2024); Japan ~15%, Russia ~8%, Sweden ~6%, Canada ~5%. Byproduct of Cu refining limits independent supply growth.
nodes.substitution: CdTe PV competes with Si PV (functional substitute). Thermoelectrics: Bi2Te3 dominant but Skutterudites and Half-Heuslers in development. II-VI semi uses small volume.
nodes.policy_context: No current export controls; mentioned in China's 2024 strategic minerals watchlist but no formal restriction.

nodes.rationale: South Africa ~93% of mined PGM/Ru (Johnson Matthey PGM Market Report 2024); Russia ~7%. Ru is critical for HDD perpendicular recording media, EUV mask absorber layers, and emerging as a high-k metal gate / interconnect candidate replacing Co/W at advanced nodes. Sole-source-by-country (SA) + no substitute for EUV mask + emerging interconnect role justifies HIGH. Not yet CRITICAL because alternatives in interconnect are R&D-stage and HDD demand declining.
nodes.concentration: South Africa ~93% of primary Ru (Johnson Matthey 2024). Russia balance. Recycling from autocatalysts/HDD media adds ~30% to global availability.
nodes.substitution: EUV mask absorber: Ru emerging as replacement for Ta-based; no near-term alternative. Interconnect: Ru competing with Co/W at <3nm — alternatives exist but Ru offers advantages. HDD: declining demand reduces criticality.
nodes.policy_context: No formal export controls. South Africa political/electrical-grid risk is operational rather than policy. Russia sanctions affect minor share.
nodes.verifier_evidence: Johnson Matthey 2025 PGM Market Report (May 2025): South Africa ~71% of primary Ru in 2025; 7th consecutive supply deficit driven by AI/data-center HDD demand. USGS Final 2025 List of Critical Minerals (Nov 2025) includes Ru but no export controls cited. SemiEngineering: Ru/Ta bilayer is investigational EUV absorber alternative; TaN/TaON remains incumbent. Applied Materials/Digitimes (Oct 2024): RuCo emerging at 2nm/3nm but not sole-source path. Phoenix Refining: industrial Ru recovery efficiencies up to 95%; recycling market USD 483M in 2025 growing 14% CAGR. LBMA/IPA: ~26% of PGM supply from recycling overall. Russia balance ~7% (proposer figure plausible). Calibration: SA 71% < Ga's 98%, no policy weaponization vs Ga's active controls — fails Gallium HIGH anchor parity; multi-refiner concentration with R&D substitution paths aligns with SiC MEDIUM anchor.

nodes.rationale: Hf is byproduct of zirconium nuclear-grade refining (Zr/Hf separation). Producers: ATI (US), Framatome (France), ChepetskyMZ (Russia), and Chinese state nuclear. HfO2 is essential for high-k gate dielectric (since 45nm) and ALD — no commercial substitute. Concentration in 3-4 producers globally + sole-use in high-k stack + nuclear industry coupling = HIGH. Not CRITICAL because supply has historically been adequate and Western producers (ATI, Framatome) dominate semi-grade.
nodes.concentration: ATI (US) + Framatome (France) + ChepetskyMZ (Russia) + CNNC (China) ~95% of nuclear-grade Hf separation. Western producers ~60-70% of semi-grade HfO2 precursors.
nodes.substitution: HfO2 high-k: ZrO2 and rare-earth oxides researched but Hf-based incumbent. ALD precursor (TEMAH, HfCl4): no functional substitute at production node. 5+ year qualification for alternative high-k.
nodes.policy_context: Russia Hf affected by post-2022 sanctions; ChepetskyMZ Western-market access constrained. No China export controls on Hf as of May 2026.
nodes.verifier_evidence: Calibration mismatch vs HIGH anchor: (1) Gallium HIGH = China ~98% + active export controls; Hafnium = Western-dominated semi-grade + zero hostile export regime. (2) Four named producers with two in NATO jurisdictions (ATI US, Framatome FR) provides genuine multi-supplier base, similar to SiC MEDIUM anchor (Wolfspeed/II-VI/SK Siltron/RoHM). (3) Substitution claim overstated: ZrO2-based high-k alternatives are researched and Zr is co-produced from same refining process — alternative chemistry pathway exists on 5yr horizon, matching MEDIUM "2-3 year qualification reach" expanded to high-k complexity. (4) Hafnium global production ~70-80 tonnes/year is genuinely small (byproduct economics, nuclear coupling) but supply-tightness risk differs from geopolitical bottleneck risk — framework rates the latter. (5) CRITICAL bars clearly fail (only multi-year qualification bar met; no ≥70% single-country share, alternatives exist). (6) HIGH bars require concentration that "forces capex to qualify alternatives outside hostile jurisdiction" — Hf concentration is already inside friendly jurisdiction, so the geopolitical lever the HIGH tier captures is absent. Verdict: DOWNGRADE to MEDIUM to maintain framework calibration consistency with SiC anchor (concentrated, multi-supplier, capex-scaling, no hostile-jurisdiction lock).

nodes.rationale: Nuclear-grade Zr (Zircaloy cladding) is concentrated in Westinghouse, Framatome, CNNC, TVEL (Russia). Semi-grade Zr usage is smaller volume (ZrO2 ALD, sputtering targets). Mineral supply (zircon sand) is ample — Australia, South Africa, Mozambique. Bottleneck is in nuclear-grade refining capacity, not raw material. Semi usage substitutable in many roles.
nodes.concentration: Zircon sand: Australia ~37%, South Africa ~30%, Mozambique ~10% (Iluka, Rio Tinto, Tronox). Nuclear-grade sponge: 4-5 global producers. Semi-grade smaller volume.
nodes.substitution: ZrO2 in semi: substitutable with HfO2 and other high-k materials. Sputtering targets: standard fabrication. Nuclear-grade cladding has no semi-stack relevance directly.
nodes.policy_context: Russia (TVEL) sanctions affect nuclear-grade for Western reactors; not semi-relevant. No export controls on semi-grade.

nodes.rationale: Helium supply has historically been volatile (US BLM reserve drawdown, Russia Amur disruptions). Producers: Air Products, Linde, Air Liquide, Messer; geographic sources: US (~50%), Qatar (~30%), Algeria, Russia, Australia. Qatar (RasGas/QatarEnergy) is dominant single-country growth source. No substitute for cryogenic cooling at 4K and below; semi uses include leak detection, fab atmosphere, MRI/MBE. Multi-country supply + multiple producers prevents HIGH classification despite periodic shortages.
nodes.concentration: US ~50%, Qatar ~30%, Algeria ~5%, Russia ~5%, Australia ~5% (US BLM data + industry reports). Qatar single-largest growth supplier. No single country >70%.
nodes.substitution: Cryogenic 4K: no substitute (only He has BP <-269C). Fab process: He partially substitutable with N2/Ar in some non-cryo roles. MRI: dry magnets emerging but slow uptake.
nodes.policy_context: Russia Amur LNG-He plant disruptions; US BLM cessation of sales (Sept 2024) tightening market. No formal export controls.

nodes.rationale: Ukraine pre-war supplied ~50-70% of global lithography-grade neon (Ingas, Cryoin in Mariupol/Odesa). Russian invasion (Feb 2022) shut both facilities; capacity has shifted to China (now ~75% by some industry estimates), Korea (POSCO/TEMC), US (Linde), and rebuilt Ukraine capacity. Concentration risk shifted from Ukraine to China + emerging dependency. Excimer laser (ArF/KrF) lithography requires high-purity Ne — no substitute. Boundary case between HIGH and MEDIUM; China dependency tilts HIGH.
nodes.concentration: Post-war: China ~70-75% (POSCO data + TrendForce 2024), Korea ~15%, US/EU/Ukraine ~10%. Pre-war Ukraine ~50%.
nodes.substitution: Excimer lithography (ArF/KrF) requires Ne — no substitute. EUV lithography does not use Ne (reduces long-term dependence). Air-separation expansion in Korea/US underway, 2-3 year qualification.
nodes.policy_context: Not under formal export controls but China dominance creates de-facto leverage. Korea building strategic reserves (announced 2023).
nodes.verifier_evidence: Proposal is a self-acknowledged boundary case (proposer confidence MEDIUM, rationale explicitly cites "boundary case between HIGH and MEDIUM"). Framework rule: "Default to MEDIUM/LOW if concentration unclear — never default to HIGH/CRITICAL." Three refutation grounds support downgrade: (1) NO formal export controls on Chinese neon — materially weaker than Gallium HIGH anchor which has binding China export controls (Aug 2023). De-facto leverage is not policy-equivalent. (2) Active diversification already commercially deployed, not merely planned: POSCO/TEMC scaled aggressively 2022-2024, Linde US capacity online, Ukraine rebuild underway, Korea strategic reserves announced 2023. This matches SiC MEDIUM anchor language ("concentrated but multi-supplier and capex scaling") more than Gallium HIGH. (3) EUV lithography does not use neon — leading-edge AI compute nodes (3nm/2nm and below) structurally bypass the dependency, capping long-term bottleneck severity. Air separation is mature technology with sub-2-year qualification, not the novel multi-year pathway required for HIGH. China 70-75% share is at the floor of the HIGH band (50-70%) and overlaps MEDIUM territory given the rapid post-2022 diversification trajectory.

nodes.rationale: Xenon is rare atmospheric gas (~0.087 ppm in air) requiring large air-separation plants for capture. Pre-2022 Ukraine and Russia ~50% combined. Post-war shifted to China (~40-50%), Korea (~25%), with US/EU smaller. Semi uses: excimer lithography (KrF/ArF still in production), ion implantation, SiOC etch. Ion thruster use (electric propulsion for space) is rising. Concentration + air-separation capacity constraint + critical semi use = HIGH.
nodes.concentration: Post-war estimates: China ~40-50%, Korea ~25%, Russia/Ukraine ~15% combined, US/EU ~15%. Air-separation byproduct limits supply elasticity.
nodes.substitution: Excimer lithography: no substitute for Xe in some laser configurations. Ion thrusters: Kr is alternative (lower performance) — SpaceX Starlink uses Kr. Semi etch: limited alternatives.
nodes.policy_context: No formal export controls. Russia/Ukraine war disrupted supply chain. China not yet weaponizing but capacity is concentrated.
nodes.verifier_evidence: Confidence per evidence weight: MEDIUM-LOW. Sources: (1) SFA Oxford xenon market profile confirms distributed production across US, Germany, Japan, Russia, China, Ukraine — no single-country dominance. (2) Asia Pacific market share cited at 34.7-37.1% in 2025 (Fortune Business Insights, IMARC, Research Nester) — this is CONSUMPTION, not production. (3) Linde Leuna, Germany xenon/krypton plant opened June 2023 — one of world's largest. (4) Air Liquide Cheonan, South Korea rare-gas purification unit inaugurated June 2025. (5) South Korea relies heavily on imports (46% of xenon imports per one source) — i.e., Korea is consumer, not 25% producer. (6) Krypton confirmed as ion thruster substitute (SpaceX Starlink). (7) ArF (193nm) lithography transition reduces Xe dependence vs older KrF. (8) No export-control regime cited — vs Ga (China Aug 2023) or Dy (China Dec 2024). Calibration: Below Ga (HIGH) anchor on every dimension (lower concentration, no policy lever, viable substitutes in primary use cases). Above Cu (LOW) — small market, byproduct economics, real war-driven volatility. Aligns with SiC (MEDIUM) anchor: concentrated production but multi-supplier with capex scaling and 2-3 year qualification paths for second sources. Calibration places at MEDIUM.

nodes.rationale: Krypton shares air-separation supply chain with Xe/Ne. Less critical for advanced semi (KrF lithography is mature/legacy node) but used in some etch and ion implantation. Used in Starlink ion thrusters as alternative to Xe. Concentration similar to Xe (China/Korea/US/EU + Russia/Ukraine disrupted). Lower semi criticality than Xe pulls rating to MEDIUM.
nodes.concentration: Similar to Xe: China ~40%, Korea ~25%, US/EU ~20%, Russia/Ukraine reduced post-war. Air-separation byproduct.
nodes.substitution: KrF lithography: legacy node, less critical than ArF/EUV. Ion thrusters: substitutable with Xe. Etch: limited but workable substitutes.
nodes.policy_context: No formal export controls. Same air-separation chain disruption as Xe/Ne.

nodes.rationale: Argon is the third most abundant atmospheric gas (~0.93%), produced abundantly via air separation globally. Air Products, Linde, Air Liquide, Messer all produce. Multi-country, multi-producer, no concentration risk. Used in sputtering and inert atmospheres in semi but fungible across suppliers. Matches LOW reference anchor (copper-like commodity gas).
nodes.concentration: Ample global supply from every major industrial gas producer; no single country >25% share. Commodity gas.
nodes.substitution: Inert sputtering atmospheres: limited alternatives (N2 in some cases) but Ar is incumbent and ample. No substitution pressure.
nodes.policy_context: No export controls, no policy risk.

nodes.rationale: WF6 is the dominant CVD precursor for W metallization in semi (contacts, vias, gates). Producers: Air Products, Linde, Versum (Merck), Kanto Denka, SK Materials, Resonac (Showa Denko), and increasingly Chinese producers. Tungsten feedstock concentration in China (~80% of W mining) + specialty-gas formulation concentrated in Japan/Korea/US creates dual chokepoint. W has no substitute in many semi metallization roles; alternatives (Co, Ru, Mo) at advanced nodes still in qualification. Boundary HIGH justified by W concentration + critical process role.
nodes.concentration: Tungsten feedstock: China ~80% (USGS 2024). WF6 production: Japan/Korea/US oligopoly (Resonac, Kanto Denka, SK Materials, Versum, Air Products) — ~6 global producers. Process gas formulation requires high purity.
nodes.substitution: W metallization: Co/Ru/Mo emerging at advanced nodes but W incumbent at <14nm legacy contact/via. Multi-year requalification. WF6 specifically: no direct substitute as W CVD precursor.
nodes.policy_context: China tungsten export licenses tightened Feb 2025 (MOFCOM). WF6 not separately controlled but upstream W feedstock risk significant.
nodes.verifier_evidence: USGS 2024 confirms China ~80-82% of global tungsten mine production, but: (1) WF6 production itself is concentrated in ALLIED jurisdictions — Resonac (JP), Kanto Denka (JP), SK Materials (KR), Versum/Merck (US/DE), Air Products (US), Linde (DE) — not China, making the "dual chokepoint" framing internally inconsistent with the China-risk thesis; (2) Cobalt has been in commercial production for contact/local interconnect at Intel 10nm/Intel 7 and TSMC N5+ since ~2018, with Ru and Mo qualified or in qualification at N3/N2 — the "no substitute" claim holds only for legacy nodes, not leading edge; (3) Global W supply includes ~30%+ recyclate from scrap, and semiconductor WF6 is a minor slice of total W demand (carbides/alloys dominate), buffering upstream feedstock risk; (4) Feb 2025 MOFCOM tungsten measure is a licensing regime, not an outright denial like Ga/Ge/Sb bans — symbolic friction rather than supply cutoff; (5) WF6 itself has no export control. Calibration: weaker than Gallium HIGH anchor (Ga = ~98% China + active denial export controls), stronger than Cu LOW. Best fit is SiC MEDIUM anchor — concentrated multi-supplier oligopoly with diversification paths and 2-3yr qualification timelines for substitutes.

nodes.rationale: SiH4 producers: Air Liquide, Linde, REC Silicon (US), Tokuyama, Mitsui Chemicals, Chinese producers. Disilane (Si2H6) is more concentrated and specialty. SiH4 used in CVD for poly-Si, SiN, SiO2 — backbone of semi. Multi-supplier base across allied jurisdictions, but specialty-gas qualification is long. Disilane is more concentrated to specialty producers. MEDIUM reflects multi-supplier base with allied concentration.
nodes.concentration: SiH4: ~6-8 global producers across US, Japan, Korea, Europe, China. Disilane: ~3-4 specialty producers (more concentrated). No single country >50%.
nodes.substitution: SiH4 for poly-Si CVD: TCS (trichlorosilane) alternative in some applications. SiN/SiO2 CVD: limited alternatives at production node. Disilane: required for ALD where higher reactivity needed.
nodes.policy_context: No formal export controls. Specialty-gas qualification creates supplier stickiness.

nodes.rationale: Electronic-grade NH3 is purified from bulk industrial ammonia (one of the largest chemical commodities globally). Multiple specialty-gas producers handle purification: Air Products, Linde, Versum, Air Liquide, Mitsui, Showa Denko, Resonac. Used in SiN CVD, nitridation. Bulk supply ample globally; purification capacity multi-supplier. No concentration risk.
nodes.concentration: Bulk NH3: global commodity, ~200 Mt/yr production across many countries. Electronic-grade purification: ~6+ global specialty producers. No concentration risk.
nodes.substitution: SiN CVD: NH3 + SiH4 standard chemistry; alternative chemistries exist for some applications.
nodes.policy_context: No export controls relevant to semi grade.

nodes.rationale: NF3 is the dominant chamber-clean gas for CVD/etch tools. Producers: SK Materials (Korea, ~40% market share), Versum/Merck (US), Kanto Denka (Japan), Resonac (Japan), Foosung (Korea), and Chinese entrants (Peric Special Gases). Korea concentration (SK + Foosung ~50%) creates some risk but multi-supplier base across allied nations. Substitution: F2-based alternatives exist for some chamber-clean roles. MEDIUM reflects Korean concentration but allied supply.
nodes.concentration: Korea (SK Materials + Foosung) ~50-55%, Japan (Kanto Denka, Resonac) ~20%, US (Versum) ~15%, China growing ~10%.
nodes.substitution: Chamber clean: F2 (fluorine gas) and ClF3 are alternatives but NF3 incumbent for safety/efficiency. Process gas: limited alternatives at production node.
nodes.policy_context: No export controls. Korean specialty gas industry well-integrated with semi customers (Samsung, SK Hynix).

nodes.rationale: Electronic-grade anhydrous HF and BHF (buffered HF) producers: Stella Chemifa (Japan, dominant), Morita Chemical (Japan), Solvay (Belgium/France), Honeywell (US), Foosung (Korea), Do-Fluoride (China). Japan + Korea + US + EU multi-country base. Fluorspar (CaF2) feedstock concentrated in China (~70%) and Mexico — upstream risk. 2019 Japan-Korea trade dispute (HF export restriction by Japan to Korea) highlighted vulnerability. MEDIUM reflects multi-supplier base with demonstrated policy risk.
nodes.concentration: Anhydrous HF semi grade: Japan ~50% (Stella, Morita), Korea ~20% (Foosung), EU ~15%, US ~10%. Fluorspar upstream: China ~65-70% (USGS).
nodes.substitution: Wet etch / oxide removal: no substitute for HF chemistry. Specialty cleans: limited alternatives. 2019 Japan-Korea episode showed Korea built domestic HF capacity within ~1 year.
nodes.policy_context: Japan 2019 HF export restriction to Korea (semi crisis). China fluorspar export controls discussed but not enacted as of May 2026. Strategic chokepoint.

nodes.rationale: SiC substrate producers: Wolfspeed (US), Coherent/II-VI (US), SK Siltron CSS (Korea), ROHM/SiCrystal (Japan/Germany), STMicro (in-house Norstel), TankeBlue (China), SICC (China). Multi-country, capex-scaling industry transitioning from 6" to 8" wafers. China capacity ramping fast (TankeBlue, SICC, SanAn, Synlight). For power semis (EV inverters, robotics motor drives, AI server PSUs) SiC is incumbent. Matches MEDIUM reference anchor (cited in framework).
nodes.concentration: Wolfspeed ~40%, II-VI ~20%, SK Siltron CSS ~10%, ROHM ~10%, Chinese producers ~15-20% growing. No single-country dominance.
nodes.substitution: GaN for higher-frequency, lower-voltage; Si for sub-1200V. SiC incumbent for 1200-3300V power. Substrate-level substitution within SiC supply pool feasible.
nodes.policy_context: No formal export controls. US CHIPS Act funding Wolfspeed expansion. China rapidly building domestic capacity.

nodes.rationale: Bulk GaN substrates (HVPE) for power GaN devices are highly concentrated: Sumitomo Electric (Japan), Mitsubishi Chemical (Japan), SCIOCS/Sumitomo Chemical, and emerging Chinese (Suzhou Nanowin, Sino Nitride). Most power GaN devices today use GaN-on-Si epi from Taiwan/US (EPC, Navitas, Innoscience) — but native GaN substrate for >900V vertical GaN requires HVPE bulk substrates. Japan dominance + thin supply + no near-term substitute for native GaN at high power = HIGH for the bulk-substrate segment.
nodes.concentration: HVPE bulk GaN: Japan (Sumitomo, Mitsubishi) ~80%+. Chinese entrants growing. GaN-on-Si epi (dominant for <650V power GaN) is broader: Taiwan, US, EU.
nodes.substitution: GaN-on-Si epi for <650V power applications (commercial scale). Native GaN required for >900V vertical and RF — no current substitute. SiC competes in 1200V+ where GaN doesn't yet scale.
nodes.policy_context: No formal export controls. Japan-allied supply for most applications. China capacity buildout strategically signaled.
nodes.verifier_evidence: Framework HIGH anchor requires (a) concentration where substitution requires capex outside HOSTILE jurisdiction AND (b) removal forces production cuts. Japan = allied to US/EU/Korea/Taiwan AI stack consumers; no export-control regime cited or in force. Commercial power GaN (<650V, the volume market) runs on GaN-on-Si epi with broad geographic supply — not on bulk HVPE substrates. GaN-on-SiC for RF has multiple Western suppliers (Wolfspeed, Coherent/II-VI). Native bulk GaN required only for narrow nascent applications (>900V vertical, some RF) that are themselves not yet at scale. SiC substrate MEDIUM anchor (Wolfspeed/Coherent/SK Siltron/RoHM/STMicro — concentrated but allied-jurisdiction multi-supplier with capex scaling) is the closer fit. Proposer's own concentration data ("Chinese entrants growing") and policy line ("No formal export controls. Japan-allied supply") undermine the HIGH calibration. MEDIUM with explicit note on bulk-HVPE sub-segment monitoring is the calibrated read.

nodes.rationale: Japan ~90%+ of EUV photoresist (JSR, TOK, Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo Chemical, Fujifilm) per multiple industry estimates (TrendForce, SEMI Japan). ArF immersion resist similarly Japan-dominated (~80%). IP and process know-how are deeply Japan-specific. No commercial substitute outside Japan for leading-edge EUV resist; qualification at fab requires 6-12 months per chemistry. JSR acquisition by JIC (Japan Investment Corp, 2023-2024) consolidated Japanese national strategic control. Meets all three CRITICAL anchors: ≥70% single-country share, no substitute today, multi-year qualification.
nodes.concentration: EUV resist: Japan ~90%+ (JSR, TOK, Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo, Fujifilm). ArF immersion: Japan ~80%, US (DuPont/Rohm and Haas, Dow) ~15%, Korea (Dongjin) ~5% emerging.
nodes.substitution: No commercial non-Japan EUV resist at leading edge. Dongjin (Korea) ArF qualification ongoing. Inpria (now JSR-owned, US-based metal oxide resist) — acquisition consolidates Japan control. Qualification 6-12 months per chemistry.
nodes.policy_context: JSR acquisition by Japan Investment Corp (METI strategic move, 2023-2024) signals Japan treating resist as strategic asset. Japan 2019 export restrictions on resist to Korea (lifted 2023) demonstrated leverage.
nodes.verifier_evidence:
CONCENTRATION (PASSES CRITICAL BAR): EUV resist Japan ~90%+ is well-documented (JSR, TOK, Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo Chemical, Fujifilm dominate qualified EUV chemistries at TSMC/Samsung/Intel leading-edge nodes). JSR's 2021 Inpria acquisition consolidated the US-based metal oxide EUV path under Japanese control. ArF immersion Japan ~80% is consistent with SEMI/TrendForce data.

SUBSTITUTION (PASSES FOR EUV, BORDERLINE FOR ArF): No commercial non-Japan EUV resist qualified at HVM for N3/N2/A14 nodes. However, DuPont/Dow hold ~15% ArF share and Dongjin Semichem (Korea) ArF qualification is progressing — meaning the ArF portion of the bundle has more substitution depth than EUV. The blended "photoresist" rating is dragged down by ArF having non-Japan options.

QUALIFICATION TIMELINE (FAILS CRITICAL BAR): Proposer states "6-12 months per chemistry" for qualification. The Dysprosium CRITICAL anchor requires "multi-year qualification path" reflecting fundamental substitution science problems (no equivalent magnetic material exists). Even a realistic photoresist requal at leading-edge fab (18-24 months including yield ramp) is 1-2 years, not the 5-10 year horizon for Dy substitution science. This is the binding calibration constraint.

JURISDICTIONAL RISK (FAILS CRITICAL BAR): The Dy CRITICAL anchor involves an adversary (China) imposing active export controls (Dec 2024) against US/allies for AI-stack-critical materials. Japan is a treaty ally, integral to the CHIPS Act-aligned semiconductor coalition. The 2019 Japan-Korea resist export episode (lifted March 2023) demonstrated leverage but was directed at Korea, not US AI stack. JSR/JIC acquisition (2024, ~$6.4B) is strategic consolidation but in an allied jurisdiction — risk profile is structurally different from Dy.

CALIBRATION VS ANCHORS: Gallium (HIGH reference) = ~98% China primary share, recyclate + ex-China diversification underway, multi-year capacity buildout for substitution. Photoresist maps cleanly onto this: severe single-country concentration, qualification capex required to onboard alternatives, but substitution paths exist on a 1-3 year horizon (Dongjin ArF expansion, Korean EUV R&D, Inpria-derived metal oxide chemistries even though now JSR-owned). Two-of-three CRITICAL anchors per framework → HIGH.

REMOVAL IMPACT: A sudden Japan resist embargo would force production cuts and emergency requalification at fabs — consistent with HIGH's "removal forces production cuts and capex to qualify alternatives" language. Not consistent with CRITICAL's "halt or severely degrade physical AI stack production within 1-2 quarters" — fabs hold strategic resist inventory and qualification of second-source chemistries is faster than rare-earth substitution science.

nodes.rationale: CMP slurry producers: Cabot Microelectronics/CMC Materials (now Entegris, US), Versum/Merck (US/Germany), Fujifilm Electronic Materials (Japan), Hitachi Chemical/Resonac (Japan), Dow (US), Soulbrain (Korea), Anji Microelectronics (China). Multi-supplier across allied nations. Slurries are recipe-formulated for specific process steps — qualification is long but supply base is diversified. Anji (China) growing share domestically. MEDIUM reflects allied multi-supplier base.
nodes.concentration: Entegris/CMC ~35%, Versum/Merck ~20%, Resonac ~15%, Fujifilm ~10%, others ~20%. US/Japan/Korea/Germany base.
nodes.substitution: Process-specific recipes; supplier substitution requires fab requalification (~6-12 months per recipe). No alternative to CMP at advanced nodes.
nodes.policy_context: No formal export controls. China Anji building domestic capacity for domestic fabs (SMIC, YMTC).

nodes.commodity: Sputtering targets (Ta, Ti, Cu, Co, Ru)
nodes.rationale: Sputtering target producers: JX Nippon Metals (Japan, dominant), Materion (US), Honeywell (US), Praxair Surface Technologies/Linde (US), Tosoh SMD (Japan/US), Plansee (Austria), Ulvac (Japan), Konfoong (China). Multi-supplier base across Japan/US/EU. Target purity and bonding to backing plates are specialty processes but multi-country supply. Tantalum and ruthenium feedstock concentration is upstream concern (Ta from DRC/Rwanda, Ru from SA). MEDIUM reflects allied multi-supplier with upstream risks.
nodes.concentration: JX Nippon ~30%, Materion ~20%, Honeywell ~15%, Tosoh ~10%, Praxair ~10%, others ~15%. Japan + US dominant.
nodes.substitution: Target fabrication is multi-supplier. Material-specific concerns: Ru (see Ruthenium entry), Ta (DRC/Rwanda concentration upstream), Co (DRC upstream).
nodes.policy_context: No export controls on targets themselves. Upstream Ta/Co/Ru feedstock has separate concentration concerns (covered elsewhere).

nodes.commodity: Synthetic fused silica / EUV mask blanks
nodes.rationale: EUV mask blanks (Mo/Si multilayer on ULE/Zerodur ultra-low-expansion glass substrates) are produced by ~3 companies globally: AGC (Asahi Glass, Japan), Hoya (Japan), Shin-Etsu Chemical (Japan). Japan ~100% of commercial EUV mask blank supply. Each ASML EUV scanner requires hundreds of mask blanks per leading-edge fab. Mo/Si multilayer deposition + defect-free polishing is multi-decade IP. No commercial substitute outside Japan; qualification of any alternative would take 3-5+ years minimum. Meets all CRITICAL anchors definitively: 100% single-country, no substitute, multi-year qualification, removal halts leading-edge logic production.
nodes.concentration: AGC + Hoya + Shin-Etsu ~100% of EUV mask blanks (Japan). Synthetic fused silica for DUV photomask substrates also Japan-dominated (~80%+).
nodes.substitution: No commercial alternative to Mo/Si multilayer EUV blanks. ULE glass substrate (Corning, US) is single-supplier upstream. Multi-decade IP for defect-free multilayer deposition. Qualification 3-5+ years for any alternative.
nodes.policy_context: Not formally export-controlled but de-facto Japan strategic asset. Allied-aligned supply mitigates near-term risk for Western fabs but creates absolute dependency.
nodes.verifier_evidence: Concentration: AGC (Asahi Glass), Hoya, Shin-Etsu Chemical collectively ~100% of EUV mask blank supply; all Japan-based (consensus across SEMI, eBeam Initiative, and SemiAnalysis reporting). Substitution: Mo/Si multilayer on ULE (Corning, US) glass substrate is the only commercial EUV mask blank architecture; no alternative chemistry at production scale; ULE substrate itself sole-sourced. Qualification timeline: 3-5+ years for any new mask blank supplier per industry standard mask qualification cycles. Policy: NOT formally export-controlled — proposal explicitly states "Not formally export-controlled but de-facto Japan strategic asset" and "Allied-aligned supply mitigates near-term risk." Framework anchor mismatch: Dysprosium CRITICAL requires hostile-jurisdiction + binding export controls (Dec 2024 China rules); Gallium HIGH describes "capex/capacity outside hostile jurisdiction" implying single-country concentration without active weaponization warrants HIGH not CRITICAL. EUV blanks satisfy concentration and substitution bars but lack the hostile-jurisdiction policy-risk vector that defines the CRITICAL anchor. Calibration-consistent rating is HIGH.

nodes.rationale: Palladium is a platinum-group metal with significant Russian concentration (Norilsk Nickel ~40% of global mine supply per Johnson Matthey 2023) plus South Africa (~38%). However, palladium trades on NYMEX/LME with deep liquidity, and substitution to platinum in autocatalysts is technically established (platinum-palladium swap accelerated post-2020 spike). For physical AI/robotics stack relevance, palladium use is narrow (sensor electrodes, MLCC terminations, hydrogen separation membranes) and not a stack-halting input. Russia sanctions risk remains but no formal export controls on Pd as of late 2025. Concentration warrants MEDIUM, not HIGH — substitution paths are commercially active.
nodes.concentration: Russia ~40% mine supply (Norilsk Nickel), South Africa ~38% (Anglo American Platinum, Sibanye-Stillwater, Impala) per Johnson Matthey PGM Market Report 2023. Combined top-2 ~78%, but two distinct jurisdictions.
nodes.substitution: Platinum substitution in autocatalysts commercially proven (Pt/Pd ratio shifted 2020-2023). Recycling supplies ~25-30% of demand. For AI-stack uses (MLCCs, sensors), nickel-based alternatives qualified.
nodes.policy_context: No formal Western export controls on Russian Pd as of late 2025; LBMA delisted Russian refiners 2022 but metal flows continue via secondary channels. Sanctions overhang creates volatility, not supply stoppage.

nodes.rationale: Uranium mine supply concentrated in Kazakhstan (Kazatomprom ~43% of global production 2023, WNA), Canada (Cameco, ~15%), Australia (~9%), Namibia (~11%). Conversion and enrichment more concentrated (Russia ~40% of global enrichment via Rosatom/TENEX, with US Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act signed May 2024 with waivers through 2027). For physical AI stack, uranium is indirect — relevant to nuclear-powered data centers and SMR roadmaps, not direct component input. Spot market exists (UxC, TradeTech) with multi-country supply. MEDIUM reflects diversification (Cameco, Orano, Kazatomprom non-Russian) and active Western capacity additions (Centrus HALEU, Urenco).
nodes.concentration: Mine: Kazakhstan ~43%, Canada ~15%, Australia ~9%, Namibia ~11% (WNA 2023). Conversion: Russia ~27% of global capacity. Enrichment: Russia ~40% (Rosatom/TENEX 2023).
nodes.substitution: No substitute for U3O8 in LWR fuel cycle, but multiple non-Russian/non-Chinese suppliers exist. Thorium fuel cycle remains R&D. For data center power, alternatives include gas, renewables + storage.
nodes.policy_context: Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act (May 2024) restricts US imports through 2040 with DOE waivers through 2027. Inflation Reduction Act + ADVANCE Act (2024) accelerating domestic conversion/enrichment.

nodes.rationale: Henry Hub is the deepest, most liquid natural gas benchmark globally (NYMEX/CME). US is world's largest natural gas producer (~25% of global output, EIA 2024) and largest LNG exporter as of 2023. For methalox propellant (Raptor, BE-4, Prometheus), the LNG-to-methane chain is multi-source with no concentration risk. Bulk industrial commodity with thousands of producers. No export control regimes constrain methane sourcing for launch. This is the textbook LOW rating — fungible, multi-country, ample.
nodes.concentration: US ~25% global production (EIA 2024), Russia ~17%, Iran ~6%, China ~5%, Canada ~5%. Henry Hub benchmark is US-centric but methane itself is globally distributed.
nodes.substitution: Methane is a chemical commodity producible from multiple feedstocks (conventional, shale, biogas, synthetic via Sabatier). For methalox launch, no substitute needed — the commodity itself is abundant.
nodes.policy_context: No export controls. US DOE LNG export approvals are policy-managed but not supply-constraining for domestic launch use.

nodes.rationale: LOX is produced via air separation units (ASUs) — the air is free, the bottleneck is energy and equipment. Major industrial gas oligopoly (Linde, Air Liquide, Air Products, Messer, Nippon Sanso) operates globally with redundant capacity. No country concentration risk; ASUs colocated near every major launch site or industrial cluster. For SpaceX, ULA, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, LOX is sourced from local industrial gas suppliers under long-term contracts. Bulk industrial commodity — LOW is the calibration anchor here.
nodes.concentration: Top-4 industrial gas majors (Linde, Air Liquide, Air Products, Messer) ~75% global merchant market but operate ASUs across all major economies. No country concentration meaningful.
nodes.substitution: No substitute for LOX as launch oxidizer in cryogenic stages, but the commodity itself is producible anywhere air and electricity exist. Not a substitution question — a production-availability question.
nodes.policy_context: No export controls. Strategic stockpile considerations for medical O2 (COVID-19 era), not launch-relevant.

nodes.rationale: Hydrazine derivatives are highly toxic, restricted under REACH (EU SVHC list 2011) and US OSHA/DOT regulations. Production is concentrated: Arch Chemicals/Lonza (US), Otsuka Chemical (Japan), Arkema (France), and Chinese producers. The market is regulated and shrinking due to ECHA restrictions and green-propellant transition (LMP-103S, AF-M315E). For satellite station-keeping and legacy launch (Ariane 5, Soyuz, Long March 2/3/4), hydrazine remains incumbent but substitution to green monopropellants is active (Astroscale, NASA GPIM mission 2019). Multi-supplier across allied jurisdictions warrants MEDIUM, not HIGH.
nodes.concentration: Producers split among Lonza (US/CH), Otsuka (Japan), Arkema (France), and Chinese chemical companies. No single country >50% for satellite-grade material. Aerospace-grade qualification is the gating factor.
nodes.substitution: Green monopropellants (LMP-103S/ECAPS, AF-M315E/ASCENT) commercially flying since 2010s. Electric propulsion (Hall thrusters, ion engines) displacing hydrazine for GEO/LEO station-keeping. 5-10 year transition underway.
nodes.policy_context: EU REACH SVHC listing (2011) restricts hydrazine; authorization required. US DOT Class 6.1 toxic + Class 8 corrosive. ECHA authorization deadlines have driven OEM transition.

nodes.rationale: N2O4/MON (mixed oxides of nitrogen) is the hypergolic oxidizer paired with hydrazine derivatives. Produced by specialty chemical suppliers — same player set as hydrazine (Air Liquide, Linde, Praxair via industrial nitric acid chains, and aerospace-qualified suppliers like Hercules/Arkema). Multi-country, multi-supplier, but aerospace-grade qualification and DOT/transport restrictions create supply chain friction. Like hydrazine, substitution path is green propellants and electric propulsion. MEDIUM tracks the pair.
nodes.concentration: Industrial N2O4 produced wherever nitric acid plants exist (global commodity). Aerospace-grade purity supplied by handful of qualified vendors (US, EU, Japan, China, Russia separately).
nodes.substitution: Substituted alongside hydrazine via green monopropellants and electric propulsion. LOX/methane and LOX/kerosene displacing hypergolic stages on new launchers (Falcon 9, Vulcan, New Glenn, Ariane 6).
nodes.policy_context: DOT Hazard Class 2.3 (toxic gas) / oxidizer. ITAR/EAR controls on aerospace-grade specifications. No country-specific export ban on industrial N2O4.

nodes.rationale: RP-1 is a tightly specified kerosene distillate fraction (MIL-DTL-25576E spec) produced by specialty refiners — Phillips 66 (Borger, TX), TimkenSteel/Calumet, and a handful of international refiners. Spec is tight but the underlying feedstock (crude oil distillate) is the most fungible commodity on earth. Falcon 9, Atlas V, Soyuz, Long March all consume RP-1 or equivalent (RG-1 in Russia). Multi-supplier, multi-country, no concentration warranting elevated rating. Distillate fraction is straightforward refinery chemistry. LOW.
nodes.concentration: US: Phillips 66 (primary SpaceX/ULA supplier), Calumet. International: Russian RG-1, Chinese equivalents. Multi-supplier across allied jurisdictions for US/EU launchers.
nodes.substitution: Methalox (Raptor, BE-4, Prometheus) displacing kerolox for new-generation launchers. RP-1 itself substitutable with refined kerosene meeting MIL-DTL-25576E from any qualified refiner.
nodes.policy_context: No export controls on kerosene. ITAR governs rocket engine designs, not fuel. Strategic Petroleum Reserve indirectly supports availability.

nodes.rationale: Liquid hydrogen production is concentrated by the industrial gas oligopoly (Air Liquide, Linde, Air Products dominate US merchant LH2 with ~80% market share, IHS Markit 2022) AND cryogenic liquefaction capacity is the actual bottleneck — NASA reported LH2 supply constraints during Artemis I delays 2022. US merchant LH2 production is ~75 tonnes/day (DOE H2A model), but liquefaction plants are few (single-digit count in North America). Substitution to LCH4 (methalox) is active for new launchers but SLS, Centaur, Vulcan upper stage, Ariane 6 upper stage all depend on LH2. Concentration in liquefaction capacity + slow capex pace warrants MEDIUM.
nodes.concentration: US merchant LH2 dominated by Air Liquide, Linde, Air Products (~80%+ combined per IHS Markit 2022). ~10 major LH2 liquefaction plants in North America. Plug Power expanding green LH2 capacity (Georgia plant 2023).
nodes.substitution: LCH4 (methalox) substituting for new-generation upper stages (Stoke Space, Relativity Terran R). SLS, Centaur V, Ariane 6 upper stage locked to LH2 for foreseeable future. Multi-year requalification path.
nodes.policy_context: Inflation Reduction Act 45V hydrogen production tax credit (Treasury final rules Jan 2025) accelerating green LH2 capacity. No export controls.

nodes.rationale: He-3 has no commercial production market at scale. Global supply is exclusively a byproduct of tritium decay from nuclear weapons stockpile maintenance — DOE Isotope Program is the dominant Western supplier, with strict allocation since 2008 shortage. Annual supply ~20-30 kg globally for all uses (cryogenics, neutron detection, medical MRI, quantum computing dilution refrigerators). Helion Energy's fusion roadmap and lunar regolith mining proposals (Interlune, Blue Origin) are speculative/Pre-commercial. Spot market exists only via DOE allocation auctions, not a continuous commodity market. Pre-commercial is the correct designation per framework.
nodes.concentration: DOE Isotope Program (US) and Russian tritium-decay stockpile are the only meaningful sources. Annual global supply ~20-30 kg estimated. Allocation-based, not market-priced at scale.
nodes.substitution: Boron-10 (BF3, B-10 lined detectors) substituted for many neutron detection applications post-2008 shortage. He-4 alternative cycles for sub-Kelvin cryogenics under R&D but inferior performance. No substitute for fusion fuel cycle if/when commercial.
nodes.policy_context: DOE Isotope Program allocation governance. No commercial export controls because no commercial market. Interlune, Helion, Blue Origin lunar-regolith proposals all 2030s+.

nodes.rationale: GOES is the high-permeability, low-loss steel used in transformer cores — directly relevant to data center power infrastructure (grid transformers, substation buildout). US production is highly concentrated: Cleveland-Cliffs (Butler, PA) is the sole domestic producer after AK Steel acquisition (2020). Globally, GOES is produced by JFE (Japan), Nippon Steel (Japan), POSCO (Korea), ThyssenKrupp Electrical Steel (Germany), Baoshan (China), NLMK (Russia). US transformer shortage 2022-2024 (DOE/Wood Mackenzie reports) was driven by GOES capacity bottleneck. Section 232 tariffs (2018) protected Cliffs but limited supply. Multi-country supply exists internationally; substitution to amorphous metal cores (Hitachi Metals/Proterial Metglas) commercially proven for distribution transformers. MEDIUM reflects real concentration + active alternatives.
nodes.concentration: US: Cleveland-Cliffs sole domestic producer post-2020. Global: Japan (JFE, Nippon Steel), Korea (POSCO), Germany (ThyssenKrupp Electrical Steel), China (Baoshan ~40% of global capacity per CRU 2023), Russia (NLMK). Top-1 country (China) ~40%, not >70%.
nodes.substitution: Amorphous metal cores (Metglas/Proterial) commercially deployed for distribution transformers, ~70-80% lower core losses but capex/process limits to smaller units. Multi-supplier international GOES available with import logistics.
nodes.policy_context: Section 232 steel tariffs (2018) protected domestic GOES production. DOE Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) program 2023-2024 funding transformer capacity. EU/UK anti-dumping duties on Chinese/Korean/Russian/Japanese GOES.

nodes.rationale: Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS) 2.5D packaging is the binding capacity constraint on AI accelerators (GPUs/HBM-bearing ASICs). TSMC is the dominant supplier and leading-edge CoWoS-L/S capacity has been reported fully booked. This is a process-capacity chokepoint, not a traded material: its scarcity is measured in monthly wafer capacity and lead time, not a country-supply share.
nodes.concentration: TSMC is the dominant CoWoS provider; monthly CoWoS capacity ~75,000-80,000 wafers (2025) scaling toward ~120,000-130,000 by end-2026. In the broader advanced-packaging market the OSAT segment (ASE, Amkor, JCET) is ~59% and foundry/IDM (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) ~39% (2025, IDC/TrendForce), but CoWoS-class 2.5D specifically remains TSMC-led. No clean single 'TSMC % of CoWoS' figure is publicly published — concentration is capacity-basis and geographically concentrated in Taiwan.
nodes.substitution: TSMC plans to outsource ~240,000-270,000 CoWoS wafers/yr to OSAT in 2026 (Amkor ~180,000-190,000; SPIL ~60,000-80,000). ASE (CoWoP), Amkor, Intel (Foveros/EMIB) and Samsung offer alternative 2.5D/3D packaging but require qualification. Supply-demand gap reported narrowing from ~20% to ~10% by end-2026 as capacity expands.
nodes.policy_context: Not export-controlled; a capacity / lead-time constraint with geographic (Taiwan) concentration risk.

nodes.rationale: Ajinomoto Build-up Film (ABF) is the dielectric beneath every high-performance flip-chip package (CPUs, GPUs, AI ASICs). The upstream film is a near-monopoly; downstream substrate conversion is a qualification-bound oligopoly. The film layer is CRITICAL-grade single-source; the node is rated HIGH pending verification of where to anchor the basis (film vs finished substrate).
nodes.concentration: Ajinomoto Fine-Techno is reported to hold ~90-95% of global ABF insulating-film supply (a near-monopoly upstream). Downstream substrate conversion is concentrated ~61% among the top three makers (Ibiden, Unimicron, Shinko; also AT&S, Nan Ya PCB). Japan / Taiwan / Austria concentrated. Figures are market-research-sourced, not USGS-grade.
nodes.substitution: No commercial substitute for ABF film at scale; glass-core substrates (Intel, Samsung, SKC) are pre-commercial. A new substrate fab costs ~$0.8-1.2B and needs ~3 years to qualify.
nodes.policy_context: Not formally export-controlled; structural single-source (Ajinomoto film) plus a capacity-bound substrate oligopoly.

nodes.rationale: Crucible-grade high-purity quartz (SiO2 >=99.9995%) is required for the quartz crucibles used to pull monocrystalline silicon ingots, plus diffusion tubes and chamber components. Feedstock is sourced almost entirely from a single geography (Spruce Pine, NC) with no known alternative large-scale deposit — a single-point-of-failure exposed by the 2024 Hurricane Helene shutdown.
nodes.concentration: >90% of the world's high-purity-quartz feedstock comes from Spruce Pine, North Carolina. The top two producers — Sibelco (Unimin) and The Quartz Corp — together account for ~75-85% of semiconductor-grade HPQ supply. No alternative large-scale deposit of comparable purity is known. Single-geography (not single-country-policy) concentration.
nodes.substitution: No commercial substitute deposit; synthetic HPQ exists but not at the scale/cost required for crucibles. Hurricane Helene (Sept 2024) halted Spruce Pine operations, with The Quartz Corp reporting no visibility on restart timelines — a direct demonstration of the concentration risk.
nodes.policy_context: US-domestic supply (not China-controlled), but extreme single-geography physical concentration. Sibelco has announced ~$200M then a further ~$500M (2024-2027) Spruce Pine expansions.
